units.translation: which the scholiast explains: they will be punished in their very bodies, the gods having visited their wrath upon them.
There is no envy, but I hesitate to trouble your mind.
But the god will have envy of their bodies,
not understanding the deceit of the Greek man nor the envy of the gods.
nor will there be envy in silence.
It is dear to honor the fortunate man without envy.
May no envy of the gods cast from afar its eye.
they will be punished in their very bodies, the gods having visited their wrath upon them
and bringing as a dowry destruction to Ilium.
ἐς φθόρον [to destruction] is a formula of execration.
Will you not keep silent and endure these things to your destruction?

where, since the meter requires the penultimate syllable to be short, I restored φιλοστόνων [loving lamentation], whose adverb φιλοστόνως [with love of lamentation] Aeschylus used at Sept. 279. The easiest emendation would be φιλαιακῶν [loving wailing], if the use of the word αἰακή [wailing] were sufficiently established, which Arcadius mentioned at p. 107, 2: on which see what I said in my notes on the tragic poets.
For by dying I am freed from wailing-loving evils,
For the people are prone to blame from the beginning.
and to cease from a humanity-loving disposition.
Such things you gained from your humanity-loving disposition.
Alas, the bed and the husband-loving paths.
I am not ashamed to speak to you of my husband-loving ways.
With infinitive: to love, i.e. to be accustomed
where Weilius conjectured φίλον [dear] (i.e. ἔθος ἐστίν [it is customary]) (Revue critique 1876 nr. 3 p. 49), which is not to be approved.

Corruptly at Suppl. 812 βίαια μὴ φιλεῖς ὁρῶν ὄμμασιν ἐνδίκοις [you do not love to see violent things with just eyes] (the words ὄμμασιν ἐνδίκοις [with just eyes] were omitted by the printer's error in the tragic poets), where Weilius conjectured φαιδροῖς [bright], Hermannus στέρξης [you would love] (to which the gloss φιλήσης [you would love] was attached).
with a double whip, which Ares loves.
Since you love this man, and hate the one you ought to love.
Indeed, I love them, and these things are not loathsome to me.
For he is idle in shameful things, but is accustomed not to be base.
He is accustomed to be silent or to speak what is timely.
He is accustomed to fear everything,
Insolence is accustomed to beget insolence.
Night is accustomed to bring forth pain to the helmsman.
But Ares is accustomed always to pluck the best flowers of the army.
God is accustomed to hasten with the one who toils.
having approached her father and thrown her arms around him, she will kiss him.
you do not love to see violent things with just eyes
O ungrateful one, for the many kisses.
I led under the chariot bridle-accustomed horses.
She lies, the lover of this man.
For this friendly order has come.
